newsitem.title: USA: U.S. farm leader attacks biotech crop opponents.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farm leader attacks biotech crop opponents.

text.p: Opponents of biotechnology in farming have no scientific grounds, ignore demands by the public for fewer chemicals in farming and may unwittingly condemn poor nations to subsistence diets if crop output cannot grow, a key U.S. farm industry leader said on Tuesday.

"Those who oppose biotechnological advances shackle the world's poor to starvation and condemn citizens of subsistence nations to shorter-than-necessary lifetimes dominated by hardscrabble work," American Farm Bureau Federation president Dean Kleckner said in a statement.
Kleckner, who participated in the World Food Summit last week in Rome, did not specify any groups as biotech opponents.

But the statement did note "isolated rumblings in Europe and elsewhere" where the environmental group Greenpeace has been leading efforts in recent weeks to boycott consumption of "Roundup Ready" soybeans, a genetically altered crop produced this year in the United States in limited quantities.
Greenpeace and others are pushing for labelling of such crops for consumers, a position opposed by the U.S. government and the farming industry as unnecessary and unworkable.

"It is impossible to segregate them," said Kleckner. "But even if they are produced scientifically to look differently or carry out unique purposes, when science approves them as safe they should not be subject to labelling or segregation requirements that falsely imply otherwise."
The European Union has approved the genetically altered crops for consumption and import, but anti-biotech sentiment in countries like Germany has grown.
Greenpeace has gathered 120,000 signatures on a petition in Germany opposing the genetically altered U.S. soybeans.
Kleckner said governments should not be swayed by consumer scares and had a long-term stake in supporting biotechnology on humanitarian, environmental and policy grounds.
"Non-tariff barriers cannot be tolerated," Kleckner said.

"These genetically altered crops are perfectly safe for humans. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency says there is no foreseeable health hazard to humans. That is quite an endorsement but it comes after mainstream, ethical scientists have extensively studied the seeds and judged them safe."

Roundup Ready soybeans were developed to be resistent to a specific herbicide. New types of corn and cotton, genetically altered to resist crop pests, were also planted this year. In all, about two million acres of the 160 million acres planted to those three crops used genetically-altered seed this year.
Kleckner said the new biotech crops would lessen the use of herbicides in farming and also mean less acres would have to be devoted to crop production.
"The mission of the world's farmers is as clear as our conscience," Kleckner said. "Improved seed quality through biotechnology will be one more tool in our toolbox to feed the world."
